Predicates:
SpillsFood(x) ::: x spills a lot of food on their clothing.
NotablyTidy(x) ::: x is notably tidy.
ClumsyFoodie(x) ::: x is a clumsy foodie who goes out frequently to find new food restaurants.
People(x) ::: x is a person.
Cleanly(x) ::: x is cleanly.
ValuatesOrderAndSpotlessness(x) ::: x values order and spotlessness.
FamilyPrioritizes(x, y) ::: x’s family prioritizes y.
Peter ::: Peter.
Premises:
∀x (SpillsFood(x) → ¬NotablyTidy(x)) ::: If people spill a lot of food on their clothing, then they are not notably tidy.
∀x (ClumsyFoodie(x) → People(x) ∧ SpillsFood(x)) ::: All clumsy foodies who go out frequently are people who spill food.
∀x (Cleanly(x) → NotablyTidy(x)) ::: If people are cleanly, then they are notably tidy.
∀x (ValuatesOrderAndSpotlessness(x) → Cleanly(x)) ::: If people value order and spotlessness, then they are cleanly.
∀x (FamilyPrioritizes(y, order_and_spotlessness) ∧ FamilyPrioritizes(z, order_and_spotlessness) ∧ FamilyPrioritizesFamily(y)) ::: All people whose families prioritize order and spotlessness themselves value order and spotlessness.
(PeterSpillsFood ∧ CleanlyPeter) ∨ (¬SpillsFoodPeter ∧ ¬CleanlyPeter) ::: Peter is either a person who spills food and is cleanly, or does not spill food and is not cleanly.
Conclusion:
(PeterSpillsFood ∧ CleanlyPeter) ∨ (FamilyPrioritizesFamilyPeter) ::: Peter is either a clumsy foodie who goes out frequently to find new food restaurants, or someone whose family prioritizes order and spotlessness.
